1030.title: Stripping the altar
1030.hook: on Maundy Thursday night, altars are stripped bare while Psalm 22 is read
1030.howItsDone: In Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and some other churches, the altar is stripped at the end of the Maundy Thursday service, sometimes while Psalm 22 is said or sung, and the congregation leaves in silence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, alabaster: a fig tree, a cleared temple court, and a jar broken open at Bethany. Your line was the quiet before. What small job did you do unseen? Day one thousand thirty.

The last hymn ends, and nobody moves toward the door. Up front, someone begins taking things off the altar. The candles go. The book goes. Then the cloths, the white linen, folded and carried out one at a time, until the table is plain wood or stone. In some churches, a voice reads a psalm while it happens, slow and steady: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The lights go down. People leave without music. It's Thursday night in Holy Week, the night of the Last Supper. Today, stripping the altar.

Thursday begins full. In the Gospels it's the night of a meal: bread broken, a cup passed, and in John, Jesus kneeling to wash his friends' feet. Then they walk out to a garden, and it all comes apart. Churches that keep the stripping of the altar end that night's service by taking the table back to nothing. They don't explain it with one meaning, and the psalm they read shows why. Psalm 22 opens with the cry Jesus will make from the cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Further down, the psalm says: "They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture." John says that's exactly what the soldiers did at the cross, dividing his clothes and gambling for his coat. So some hear the bare altar as Jesus himself, stripped. Others hear it as the friends who left him. Mark puts it in one hard line about the garden: "And they all forsook him, and fled." The table that was crowded earlier that night is empty, the way the garden emptied. And some simply hear it as the start of waiting. In the churches that do this, the table stays bare into Good Friday, and it isn't dressed for a feast again until Easter. The point isn't gloom for its own sake. It's honesty about the night. The psalm doesn't stay in despair, either; it turns, later on, toward praise. But the service stops before the turn. It leaves you with the bare wood, and lets Friday come.

Here's the practice: clear a table completely. Any table near you, or a desk, or a nightstand. Take everything off, one thing at a time, and set it somewhere else. The cloth or mat too, if there is one. Then stop and look at the bare surface. Settle, and breathe. Notice the grain, the marks, the scratches you usually cover up. If you pray, you can read the first line of Psalm 22 slowly, once. If you don't, just stay with the empty surface for the time, without filling it. The bell holds the time.
Vesture. Old word for clothing, named in Psalm 22 where soldiers cast lots for it at the cross, read on the night the altar is stripped bare.
Your line: bare. Today, leave one surface empty, and let it stay that way until Sunday. Day one thousand thirty.

1031.title: The Stations of the Cross
1031.hook: fourteen stops along the way of the cross, prayed in some churches
1031.howItsDone: Catholics, Anglicans and some other Christians pray the Stations of the Cross, especially on Good Friday, walking from station to station in church with a short reading and prayer at each.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vesture: a table cleared to the wood while a psalm was read in the dark. Your line was bare. What surface did you leave empty? Day one thousand thirty-one.

Along the side walls of some churches hang small carvings or paintings, spaced out like mile markers. A man standing before a judge. A woman holding out a cloth. A stranger pulled from the crowd to carry a beam of wood. On Good Friday, and in some churches on other Fridays too, people walk from one to the next. They stop, they pray, they move on. In Jerusalem, pilgrims walk a route through the old streets that tradition calls the way of sorrows, stopping at the same scenes. On a church wall, the walk comes to wherever you live. Today, the Stations of the Cross.

The stations are a walk with stops. Tradition counts fourteen in the usual set, starting with Jesus condemned and ending with his body laid in the tomb. Some of the stops come straight from the Gospels. Others come from tradition. Take one from the Gospels first. Luke says that as they led Jesus away, the soldiers grabbed a passerby. In the King James: "they laid hold upon one Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and on him they laid the cross, that he might bear it after Jesus." A man on his way into the city, minding his own business, ends up walking directly behind Jesus with the weight on his shoulders. Some readers hear in that phrase, after Jesus, the language of following. Then, a little further on, Luke has women in the crowd weeping, and Jesus turns to them: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children." Even on that road, he turns to face them, and his words point past his own suffering to troubles still ahead for the city and its children. Other stations, like Jesus falling under the cross, or a woman named Veronica wiping his face, come from tradition rather than the Gospel text. The stations are prayed in Catholic and Anglican churches, and in some others. Some versions use only scenes found in the Gospels, and some Protestants prefer it that way. Whichever set is used, the shape is the same. You don't take in the whole story at once. You walk a few steps, you stop at one moment, you stay with it, and then you walk again. It's the story at walking pace.
screen: `SOME FROM THE GOSPELS, SOME FROM TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk and pause fourteen times. Around the room is enough, or down a hallway, or in place if you need to. Take a few slow steps, and stop. One breath. Then walk again. At each stop, let one face come to mind: someone carrying something heavy right now. Don't count too carefully, and don't hurry. If you pray, you can name each person to God at each stop. If you don't, simply hold them there for one breath, the way Simon held the beam. The bell holds the time.
Cyrenian. The name for Simon, the passerby soldiers pulled from the crowd to carry Jesus's cross, walking it one station at a time.
Your line: step by step with him. Today, when something feels too heavy to face whole, take it one stop at a time, and pause between the stops. Day one thousand thirty-one.

1032.title: The three hours
1032.hook: some churches keep noon to three on Good Friday with his seven last words
1032.howItsDone: Some churches hold a Good Friday service from noon to three, with readings, hymns, silence and short meditations on each of the seven sayings of Jesus from the cross; people may stay for part or all of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyrenian: a walk with stops, and Simon carrying the beam behind Jesus. Your line was step by step with him. What did you take one stop at a time? Day one thousand thirty-two.

"Now from the sixth hour there was darkness over all the land unto the ninth hour." That's Matthew, in the King James Bible, describing the afternoon of the crucifixion. The sixth hour to the ninth: on our clocks, around noon to three. On Good Friday, some churches keep exactly those hours. The doors stay open. People come in on a lunch break and leave again, or sit through the whole afternoon. There are readings, a few hymns, and long stretches of silence. And running through it, one at a time, are the things Jesus said from the cross. Today, the three hours.

Start with the texts themselves. No single Gospel has all of them. Tradition gathers seven sayings from the four Gospels and sets them in an order. In Luke, Jesus says, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." To a criminal crucified beside him, who asks to be remembered, he says, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." In John, he looks down at his mother and his friend: "Woman, behold thy son!" and to the friend, "Behold thy mother!" Then the cry Matthew and Mark both keep: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" the first line of Psalm 22. Back in John: "I thirst." Then: "It is finished." And Luke's last: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Now look at the shape the order makes. The first three words are for other people: the ones killing him, a stranger dying next to him, his mother. In that much pain, he's still giving things away. Then the dark center, the cry of being forsaken, prayed in the words of a psalm. Then the body: thirst. Then the work done. Then trust. Christians hear different things in the sayings, and the churches that keep the three hours may preach on each in turn. But the order alone teaches something. It moves from others, through abandonment, to rest in God's hands. The three hours give each word room, so none of them gets rushed.

Here's the practice: read the seven words. Slowly, with one breath between each, aloud or under your breath. Forgive them, for they know not what they do. Today, paradise. Behold thy son. Behold thy mother. Why hast thou forsaken me. I thirst. It is finished. Into thy hands. Then go back to whichever one caught on something, and stay with it for the rest of the time. If you pray, you can let it become your prayer. If you don't, just let it sit with you. The bell holds the time.
The three hours. Noon to three on Good Friday, kept in some churches with silence, readings, and the seven words from the cross.
Your line: the seven words. Today, choose one of the seven and carry it with you until three o'clock this afternoon, or tomorrow's if three has passed. Day one thousand thirty-two.

1033.title: The harrowing of hell
1033.hook: the Orthodox Easter icon: Christ breaking the gates of death and pulling Adam and Eve up by the wrists
1033.howItsDone: Orthodox churches display the icon of the resurrection, which shows Christ breaking the gates of death and raising Adam and Eve, at Easter; Western churches that use the Apostles' Creed say its line about the descent, and some remember it on Holy Saturday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three hours: noon to three in the dark, and seven words from the cross. Your line was the seven words. Which one did you carry? Day one thousand thirty-three.

The doors are broken. In the icon, two heavy gates lie flat on the ground, and scattered around them are keys, bolts and broken locks. Christ stands on the fallen doors, dressed in white, and he's reaching down with both hands. On one side an old man is being pulled up out of a tomb. On the other, an old woman. Adam and Eve. And look at the hands. He isn't holding theirs. He has them by the wrists, the way you'd pull someone out of deep water. This is the icon Orthodox Christians set out for Easter. Its story belongs to the Saturday in between. Today, the harrowing of hell.

Holy Saturday is the day the Gospels leave almost silent. The body is in the tomb. Luke says the women who had followed Jesus rested on the sabbath, as the law asked. And that's nearly all. So where was he? Christians answered from a handful of lines. One is in First Peter, which says that Christ, put to death in the flesh, went and preached to spirits in prison. In the King James: "By which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison." Another is the old creed, which in the Book of Common Prayer runs: "He descended into hell; The third day he rose again from the dead." In the icon, hell means the place of the dead, where those who died before him wait. And a psalm gives the picture of the doors: "For he hath broken the gates of brass, and cut the bars of iron in sunder." Put together, it's a rescue story. In that picture, death is a prison, and on the Saturday the one who died goes in, breaks the gates from the inside, and starts pulling people out, beginning with the first two in the whole human story. That's why the wrists matter. Adam and Eve don't climb out by hanging on tight. They're held. Orthodox Christians and Catholics both keep this teaching, and Anglicans and Lutherans who use the Apostles' Creed say its line. Some Protestant readers take First Peter in other ways, and some churches say the creed as he descended to the dead. The icon doesn't settle those debates. It just shows the hands.

Here's the practice: look at the icon of the resurrection. If you can, find an image of it; it's often called the Anastasis. If not, hold the picture from a minute ago in mind. Settle, and breathe. Look first at the broken doors underfoot. Then at the hands, closed around the wrists. Then at the faces of Adam and Eve, old and tired and being lifted. Notice where your eye wants to rest, and let it rest there. If you pray, you can simply look, and let the looking be prayer. If you don't, stay with the image for the time. The bell holds the time.
The harrowing of hell. The teaching that on Holy Saturday Christ went down to the dead, broke the gates, and brought them out, with Adam and Eve first.
Your line: he pulls them out. Today, if someone near you is stuck, offer help that doesn't depend on them asking for it well. Day one thousand thirty-three.

1034.title: The Easter vigil
1034.hook: a fire, a great candle, and an ancient song, the Exsultet: this is the night
1034.howItsDone: Catholics, Anglicans, Lutherans and some other churches keep the Easter Vigil on Saturday night: a new fire, the Easter candle carried into the dark church, the Exsultet sung, readings from the Hebrew Bible, and sometimes baptisms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the harrowing of hell: broken gates underfoot, and Adam and Eve pulled up by the wrists. Your line was he pulls them out. Who did you reach toward? Day one thousand thirty-four.

Saturday night, after dark, and the church is pitch black. Outside the door, a small fire is burning, and people stand around it in their coats. A tall candle is lit from the fire and carried in, and a voice sings out: the light of Christ. The people answer: thanks be to God. Everyone is holding a little candle, and the flame is passed from the tall one, hand to hand, until the dark room is full of small lights. Then, in the candlelit church, someone sings an old song called the Exsultet. One line keeps coming back in it, again and again. This is the night. Today, the Easter vigil.

A vigil is a night spent awake, waiting. This one waits for Easter, and it starts in the dark on purpose. Then comes the song. The Exsultet opens by calling heaven and earth to rejoice. Then it turns into a list, and line after line begins the same way: this is the night. This is the night, it sings, when God brought Israel out of Egypt and through the sea. This is the night when a pillar of fire drove back the darkness. This is the night when Christ broke the chains of death and rose. The song reaches back to the book of Exodus, which says of the night Israel left Egypt, in the King James: "It is a night to be much observed unto the LORD for bringing them out from the land of Egypt." Jewish families keep that night at the Passover table with their own telling of the story. The vigil takes up the same night and sets the empty tomb inside it. Then the Exsultet says something daring. It calls Adam's sin a happy fault, because of the rescue it led to. Yesterday's icon, sung. After the song, in churches that keep the full vigil, it reads story after story from the Hebrew Bible by candlelight: creation, the sea, the prophets. Then the church fills with light. In churches that set the alleluia aside for Lent, it comes back tonight. Some churches baptize new Christians at this service. The candle carries a line from John's Gospel into the room: "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."

Here's the practice: light a candle in the dark. Turn the lights off, or as many as you can, and light one candle somewhere safe. If there's no candle, use the smallest light you have. Settle, and breathe. Watch how far one small flame reaches. Notice the edges of the room you can and can't see. If you pray, you can say the vigil's line quietly: this is the night. If you don't, simply stay with the one light and the dark around it. The bell holds the time.
Exsultet. The ancient song sung by candlelight at the Easter vigil, repeating this is the night as it tells the story of rescue.
Your line: this is the night. Tonight, before you sleep, sit for one minute in the dark with a single small light on. Day one thousand thirty-four.

1035.title: Sunrise service
1035.hook: Protestants often gather outdoors at dawn on Easter morning
1035.howItsDone: Some Protestant congregations hold an Easter sunrise service outdoors, on a hill, in a park or churchyard, with hymns and the Gospel reading of the empty tomb as the sun comes up; some Moravian congregations hold theirs in their burial grounds.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Exsultet: a fire by the door, one tall candle, and a song that kept saying this is the night. Your line was this is the night. What did one small light show you? Day one thousand thirty-five.

Folding chairs on wet grass, set out in rows facing east. A hillside, a park, a beach, a churchyard. It's cold and still mostly dark, and people are arriving in coats with blankets and thermoses, talking in low voices. A guitar is being tuned somewhere, or a little brass band is warming up. Nobody has lit a candle. They're waiting for the sun. Then, as the sky over the hill goes from gray to pink, they start to sing. Some Protestant churches gather like this on Easter morning, outdoors, timed to the dawn. Today, the sunrise service.

Why dawn? Because that's when the Gospels say the women went to the tomb, and they don't all describe the light the same way. Mark, in the King James, says they came "very early in the morning the first day of the week" and "at the rising of the sun." John says Mary Magdalene came "early, when it was yet dark." One has the sun coming up, the other has it still dark. A sunrise service sits right in that gap, in the half-light between them. Now stay with John's version, because it's built on that half-light. Mary finds the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. She stands outside weeping. A man speaks to her, and she takes him for the gardener and asks where they've put the body. Then, in the King James: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." She doesn't know him by his face. She knows him when he says her name. Tradition traces the outdoor dawn service to Moravian Christians, and some Moravian congregations still gather in their graveyards at sunrise on Easter, among the graves, to sing. Other churches gather on hillsides, in parks, on beaches. The setting changes. The hour doesn't. People get up in the cold and stand in the dark on purpose, the way the women did, and wait for it to get light.
screen: `SHE KNOWS HIM WHEN HE SAYS HER NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a sunrise. If it's dawn where you are, go to a window that faces the light. If it isn't, turn toward the brightest window or lamp nearby, or close your eyes and remember a sunrise you've seen. Settle, and breathe. Notice how slowly the light comes: gray first, then color. Nothing about it hurries. If you pray, you can sit in the quiet the way Mary stood at the tomb, listening. If you don't, simply watch the light, or remember it, for the time. The bell holds the time.
Sunrise service. An Easter service held outdoors at dawn, at the hour the Gospels say the women came to the tomb.
Your line: early, while it was dark. Tomorrow, or the next clear morning, get up early enough to watch the sky change, even for one minute. Day one thousand thirty-five.

1036.title: Orthodox Pascha
1036.hook: at midnight: Christ is risen! Truly he is risen! and eggs dyed red for his blood
1036.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians keep Pascha with a midnight service: the light passed from one candle, the greeting "Christ is risen!" answered "Truly he is risen!", and a meal afterward that breaks the fast, with eggs dyed red. The date can fall on a different Sunday from Western Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sunrise service: chairs on wet grass facing east, and Mary hearing her name in the half-light. Your line was early, while it was dark. Did you catch the sky changing? Day one thousand thirty-six.

"Christ is risen!" A priest shouts it at midnight from the doors of a church, and the crowd packed outside shouts back: "Truly he is risen!" He calls it again. They answer again. Over and over, in whatever language the parish prays. A little while ago the church was dark; now every hand holds a lit candle, and the bells are going. Old men shout it. Children shout it louder. When the service is over, people go home to break the long fast, and on the table, in a bowl, are eggs dyed deep red. Today, Orthodox Pascha.

Start with the name. Paul writes, in the King James: "For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us." The Greek word behind passover there is pascha, and it's the word Orthodox Christians use for Easter itself. The feast is the Passover of Christ, from death to life. Now the call and answer. Luke says that on the first Easter evening, when two friends came back to Jerusalem from Emmaus, the disciples met them with: "The Lord is risen indeed." Pascha turns that into a greeting with two voices. One person says it, and someone else has to say it back. The news isn't finished until a second voice agrees. Through the night the choir sings a short hymn again and again: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs. Trampling down death by death. Not escaping it. Walking through it and breaking it from the inside, the way the icon shows him standing on the broken gates. Then a sermon is read that tradition credits to John Chrysostom. It invites everyone to the feast: those who kept the fast, and those who didn't; those who came early and those who came at the last hour. Let no one fear death, it says. Then the eggs. Tradition says the red is for the blood of Christ, and the shell is the sealed tomb that breaks open. There's a story people tell about Mary Magdalene and an egg that turned red, but it isn't in the Gospels. In some places people tap their eggs together, one saying Christ is risen, the other answering, to see whose cracks.

Here's the practice: dye or decorate an egg. If you have one, hold it and mark it, even with a pen: a cross, a line, a little color. If you don't, hold any small, smooth thing. Settle, and breathe. Feel the shell, closed and still, made to be broken open. If you pray, you can say the old greeting under your breath, both halves: Christ is risen. Truly he is risen. If you don't, simply notice what the egg is like, sealed now, and meant to open. The bell holds the time.
Orthodox Pascha. Easter as Orthodox Christians keep it: a midnight call of Christ is risen, the answer truly he is risen, and red eggs at the end of the fast.

Your line: truly he is risen. This week ran from a bare altar, through the stations and the seven words, the broken gates, the fire and the dawn, to midnight. Today, when someone tells you good news, be the second voice: say it back. Day one thousand thirty-six.

what a scholar hears: Paul's "Christ our passover" uses the word pascha (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the answer echoes Luke 24:34, "the Lord is risen indeed."

sources.ref: Paschal homily attributed to John Chrysostom
